transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

I guess what finally pushed me to come in is that I don’t really feel like myself anymore. Not in a dramatic way, exactly, but more like… the part of me that used to naturally reach for people, or get excited about things, has gone very quiet.

I still do what I’m supposed to do, mostly. I go through obligations, I show up where I need to, but it feels kind of mechanical. I used to really take pleasure in my work, and yoga, and going to galleries, even journaling — those were things that helped me feel connected to myself. And lately it’s like I can’t quite access that. I’m doing the motions, but there’s not much there behind it. That’s what scared me enough to make the appointment.
Did this start after a specific stressful event or major life change?

Yes… I think there was a point where it started, or at least where I can trace it back to. It’s been about eight months now, maybe a little over, since we took my older relative into our apartment. That was the big change.

I don’t know if I noticed it immediately in a clean way, like “oh, this is when everything changed,” but looking back, that’s when this whole shift in how I’m thinking and working and connecting with people really began. It’s like my mind got more crowded, and at the same time I started feeling more distant from people and from the things I usually relied on. At first I told myself it was just the adjustment, because having another person in the apartment changes the whole rhythm of the place, and I thought I’d adapt. But it’s been months now, and it hasn’t really gone back to normal.
Over the past couple of weeks, have you been feeling down or depressed most days?

I’m not sure I would call it “depressed,” exactly. That word feels a little too simple for what it’s been like. Over the past couple of weeks, I’ve had days where I feel flat or sort of muted, like things don’t really land emotionally the way they used to. But if you mean sad all day, crying, that kind of obvious heaviness… no, not most days in that clear way.

It’s more that I wake up and there’s this sense of effort around everything, and I keep wondering if I’m just tired or overwhelmed. I can still get through the day, and sometimes I can seem fine from the outside, so it’s hard for me to know how to answer. I wouldn’t say I’ve felt happy, exactly, but “down most days”... maybe somewhat, but not in a way I can neatly label.
Over the past two weeks, have you lost interest or pleasure in things you usually enjoy?

Yes… I think that’s probably the biggest part of it, honestly. It’s not that I never do those things anymore, but the feeling I used to get from them is just… much quieter, almost absent sometimes.

Work used to give me a real sense of meaning, even on hard days. I could feel engaged, like I was connected to people and doing something that mattered. Now I still show up, I still go through what I’m supposed to do, but it feels more like I’m completing tasks than actually being there in the way I used to be.

And outside of work, it’s similar. Yoga used to help me feel grounded, galleries used to make me curious, journaling used to feel like I was sorting myself out. Lately I either don’t reach for those things, or if I do, I’m kind of just… performing the habit. Like I know they’re things I used to enjoy, so I try them, but I don’t get much pleasure from them. Even with people, I don’t naturally reach out the way I used to. I’m mostly just moving through obligations.
Have you been worrying a lot more than usual lately?

I don’t know if I’d say “worrying a lot more,” exactly. I mean, I do think about things a lot, and I can get stuck turning things over in my head, but I’m not sure it feels like ordinary worry in the way I would usually describe it.

When I think of worrying, I think of being anxious about bills, or someone’s health, or whether I made a mistake at work, that kind of thing. This feels harder to categorize. Some days I’m preoccupied, definitely, and I can spend too much time trying to make sense of things or replaying conversations or wondering what I’m missing. But I don’t know that I’ve noticed a clear increase in worry, like constant anxious fear.

So… maybe some, but I’m not sure. I wouldn’t want to overstate it.
Have these changes started to interfere with how well you function in daily life?

Yes… though I’ve been trying not to admit that, I think. I’m still showing up to work, so part of me wants to say I’m functioning, because I’m not, you know, staying home or completely falling apart. I get dressed, I go in, I see people, I answer emails. From the outside it probably looks like I’m basically doing my job.

But I’m definitely not functioning at my usual level. I’ve missed some grant deadlines, which is really unlike me. That’s the kind of thing I normally keep track of almost automatically, or at least I used to. And my supervisor hasn’t made a big dramatic issue of it, but I’ve noticed she’s quietly moved some of my more demanding clients to other clinicians. She framed it very gently, like redistributing caseloads, but I know what it means. Or at least I think I do. It’s because I’m not as sharp or as present as I usually am.

So yes, it is interfering. Not in a catastrophic way, maybe, but enough that other people are adjusting around me, and that feels… embarrassing. And worrying, honestly.
Do you feel that these changes are mainly because of taking your older relative into your home?

Yes… I think so. I mean, I don’t want to make it sound like I’m blaming them, because that feels awful and unfair, and it’s more complicated than that. But the timing is pretty clear to me.

This whole change in how I’m thinking, and how I’m working, and how connected I feel with people has been going on for about eight months, which is basically since we took my older relative into our apartment. At first I thought it was just an adjustment period, you know, everyone needing to get used to the new routines and less space and the emotional weight of it. I kept telling myself it would settle.

But it hasn’t really gone back to normal. It feels like that was the point where things shifted, and I’ve been kind of moving through life differently since then. So yes, I do think it’s mainly connected to that, or at least it started around then.
For most of the last eight months, have you felt sad or down nearly every day?

I don’t think so… not nearly every day, no. I mean, I’ve had days where I feel heavy or discouraged, especially when I’m aware that I’m not keeping up the way I usually do, and that can feel pretty awful. But I wouldn’t describe the last eight months as me being sad or down most days.

It’s more like… I get tired of myself, or frustrated, or unsettled. There are moments where I feel low, definitely, but then other days I’m just trying to get through things and I’m not necessarily sad. So if you mean a persistent depressed mood almost every day, I don’t think that fits exactly.
Over the past six months, have you felt anxious or on edge more days than not?

I’m not sure I’d describe it that way exactly. I mean, I’ve definitely felt tense at times, and there are days when I feel sort of wound up or watchful, like I’m waiting for something to go wrong. But “more days than not” over six months… I don’t know. That feels hard to say.

I think I’d have to really look back and count it, because some weeks feel worse than others, and then other times I’m just distracted or tired or preoccupied, not necessarily anxious. So I wouldn’t want to say yes too strongly if you mean a steady, almost constant anxiety. I’ve noticed stress, definitely, but I’m not sure it’s been that frequent in the way you’re asking.
Does having your older relative living with you still feel like an ongoing source of stress for you?

I guess… yes, in some ways it still does, but I’m not sure I can separate out how much of the stress is specifically from them living with us versus everything that comes with that arrangement, if that makes sense.

It’s not like every single moment is stressful, and I don’t want to make them sound like the problem. They’re family, and I care about them. But having another person in the home, especially an older relative who needs consideration and has their own routines and needs, changes the whole feeling of the apartment. There’s less privacy, less quiet, less of that feeling that I can fully decompress when I get home.

So yes, I’d say it still feels like an ongoing pressure. Maybe not a crisis every day, but a kind of background strain that hasn’t really gone away.
Do you feel emotionally drained or burned out by the ongoing demands at home?

I’m not completely sure how to answer that. “Burned out” feels like a strong word, and I don’t know if I’d say that exactly. I do feel tired by it sometimes, emotionally tired, like there’s always one more thing to think about at home and I can’t quite fully relax.

But then part of me thinks, well, that’s just what family situations are like, and maybe I’m making too much of it. It’s not like I’m constantly at the end of my rope. Some days I handle it fine, or I just go through the motions and don’t think about it too much.

So… drained at times, yes, probably. But I’m not sure I’d describe it as full burnout. It’s more like this ongoing background fatigue from having to stay considerate and aware of everyone in the house.
During this past eight months, was there ever a period of two weeks in a row when you felt down or depressed most of the day nearly every day?

I don’t know if I can say that clearly. Two weeks in a row, most of the day nearly every day… that’s pretty specific, and I’d have to think hard about it.

I’ve had low days, definitely, and times where I felt worn down or kind of flat, but whether it was truly depressed most of the day almost every day for a full two weeks… I’m not sure. I don’t want to overstate it. Sometimes the days blur together, especially when there’s stress at home, and then looking back I can’t always tell if I was actually down the whole time or just tired and fed up.

So I guess my honest answer is: I’m not sure. I can’t point to a definite two-week stretch like that, but I also wouldn’t say I’ve felt great the whole time.
During the last eight months, was there ever a two-week period when you had almost no interest or pleasure in things nearly every day?

Yes… I think that’s closer to what finally made me feel like I should come in, honestly. I don’t know if I can map it perfectly onto a clean two-week block, but there have definitely been stretches where the part of me that used to reach for things has just gone very quiet.

I used to be someone who would want to connect with people, or I’d get something out of my work, even when it was hard. I’d go to yoga, or wander through galleries, or write in my journal and feel like there was some pleasure or meaning in it. Lately it’s more like I know those things are supposed to matter to me, and I can remember that they used to, but I don’t really feel pulled toward them.

It’s not that I’m refusing everything or lying in bed all day. I still do what I have to do. I show up, I handle obligations, I go through the motions. But that’s kind of the problem — it feels like mostly obligations. The interest, the enjoyment, the part of me that used to naturally lean toward life a bit… it feels muted. So yes, I’d say there have been periods where I had very little interest or pleasure nearly every day, even if I’m hesitant about the exact timing.
During those stretches when your interest and pleasure were very low, did your sleep change noticeably?

I’m not totally sure, honestly. I mean, my sleep is one of those things I don’t track very carefully unless it gets really extreme, and I don’t know that I could say there was a clear, noticeable change that lined up neatly with those stretches.

There were nights where I probably stayed up too late, but sometimes that’s just me avoiding the end of the day, if that makes sense, or getting caught in my own thoughts. And other times I’d sleep and still not feel especially refreshed. But I don’t know if that’s a sleep change exactly, or just being tired in a more general way.

So… I wouldn’t say I noticed a major change. Nothing where I thought, “Oh, I’m barely sleeping,” or “I’m sleeping all day.” It was more that the days felt kind of dull and heavy, but I can’t clearly tie that to my sleep being different.
During those periods when your interest and pleasure were very low, did your appetite change noticeably?

I don’t think so… not in a way I noticed clearly. Appetite is a little tricky for me because it can vary day to day anyway — sometimes if I’m busy or tense I’ll forget to eat until later, and other times I’ll eat something just because it’s there, not because I’m especially hungry. So I’m hesitant to say there was a real change.

During those low-interest periods, I wasn’t really thinking, “Oh, I’ve lost my appetite,” or “I’m eating much more than usual.” It was more like food became part of the general routine — make something, eat enough, move on. I don’t remember my weight changing or people commenting or anything like that.

So… no, I wouldn’t say my appetite changed noticeably. If it did shift a little, it wasn’t enough that it stood out to me.
During those periods when your interest and pleasure were very low, did you also feel unusually tired or low in energy?

I’m not sure I’d call it unusually tired, exactly. I mean… I did feel kind of drained sometimes, but it’s hard for me to separate that from just the emotional flatness of those periods, if that makes sense.

There were days where everything took more effort than it should have — answering messages, getting through work, doing normal chores — but I don’t remember it as a clear physical exhaustion, like I couldn’t get out of bed or needed to nap all the time. It was more like I had to manually push myself through things because there wasn’t much internal momentum.

So… maybe a little low energy, but I’m hesitant to say it was a big, noticeable change. It didn’t stand out to me the way the lack of interest did.
During those periods when your interest and pleasure were very low, did you have trouble concentrating?

I’m not sure I can say that I did, at least not in a clean way. Concentration is one of those things where I second-guess myself, because some days I’m focused and some days I’m not, and it depends so much on the task and how much structure there is around me.

During those low-interest stretches, I definitely had less drive to engage with things, so if something felt boring or optional, my mind would drift more easily. But I don’t know if that was concentration trouble exactly, or more that I just didn’t care enough to stay with it. Like, if I had to do something important, I could usually make myself sit down and get through it, even if it felt kind of mechanical.

I don’t remember it being a big obvious problem, like reading the same paragraph over and over or not being able to follow conversations. Nothing that stood out that strongly. So I’d say… maybe a little harder to stay engaged, but I wouldn’t say I noticed major concentration problems.
During those stretches when your interest and pleasure were very low, did you feel worthless or excessively guilty?

I don’t think so… not in the way I would understand “worthless” or “excessively guilty.” I mean, I can be hard on myself in general, and during those stretches I might think, “Why am I not doing more?” or “Why does everything feel so flat when nothing is technically wrong?” But I don’t remember it turning into this strong belief that I was a bad person or that I didn’t deserve anything.

And guilt… maybe ordinary guilt, like if I wasn’t as responsive to people or I let something sit too long, I’d feel a little bad about that. But it wasn’t this heavy, consuming guilt, like I’d done something terrible or was responsible for things beyond me. It was more frustration with myself than guilt, I think.

So no, I wouldn’t say I felt worthless. Maybe self-critical at times, but not in a severe or constant way.
At any point in the last eight months, was there a period of at least two weeks when you felt sad, down, or depressed nearly every day?

I don’t think there was a full two-week stretch like that, no. I’ve had days where I felt kind of down or emotionally heavy, and there were those periods where things felt flat and I wasn’t getting much pleasure out of things, but “sad or depressed nearly every day” feels a little different to me.

I’m trying to be careful because I know it can blur together when you look back over eight months. But when I think of actually feeling sad — like waking up most days feeling depressed, or carrying that low mood through the day — I don’t remember that happening for two weeks straight. It was more intermittent, or more like lack of interest than sadness, if that distinction makes sense.

So my best answer would be no, not that I noticed.
If your older relative were no longer living with you, do you think these symptoms would mostly go away?

I’m not sure they would mostly go away, exactly. I do think the timing is hard to ignore, because this whole change in how I’ve been thinking, working, and connecting with people has really been going on for about eight months, and that’s basically since we took my older relative into our apartment.

So part of me thinks, yes, if that living situation changed, maybe some of the pressure around it would ease up. But I don’t know that I can say everything would just return to normal automatically. It’s been long enough now that it feels like it’s affected my routines and how I move through the day, not just a temporary reaction to one bad week.

I guess my answer is: I think it’s connected to having them there, because that’s when it started, but I can’t confidently say it would all mostly disappear if they weren’t living with us anymore.

target_item.reason: The question is about whether the older relative living at home remains an ongoing stressor, but the symptom profile does not include a specific item for current psychosocial stressors or living situation stress.

patient.answer:
I guess… yes, in some ways it still does, but I’m not sure I can separate out how much of the stress is specifically from them living with us versus everything that comes with that arrangement, if that makes sense.

It’s not like every single moment is stressful, and I don’t want to make them sound like the problem. They’re family, and I care about them. But having another person in the home, especially an older relative who needs consideration and has their own routines and needs, changes the whole feeling of the apartment. There’s less privacy, less quiet, less of that feeling that I can fully decompress when I get home.

So yes, I’d say it still feels like an ongoing pressure. Maybe not a crisis every day, but a kind of background strain that hasn’t really gone away.

doctor.intent: Clarify whether the symptoms are driven by caregiving-related exhaustion rather than a depressive or anxiety disorder, by assessing emotional depletion from chronic stress.
doctor.question: Do you feel emotionally drained or burned out by the ongoing demands at home?

target_item.reason: The question is asking about emotional exhaustion or burnout related to ongoing home demands, which is not directly covered by the listed schizophrenia symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
I’m not completely sure how to answer that. “Burned out” feels like a strong word, and I don’t know if I’d say that exactly. I do feel tired by it sometimes, emotionally tired, like there’s always one more thing to think about at home and I can’t quite fully relax.

But then part of me thinks, well, that’s just what family situations are like, and maybe I’m making too much of it. It’s not like I’m constantly at the end of my rope. Some days I handle it fine, or I just go through the motions and don’t think about it too much.

So… drained at times, yes, probably. But I’m not sure I’d describe it as full burnout. It’s more like this ongoing background fatigue from having to stay considerate and aware of everyone in the house.

doctor.intent: Distinguish adjustment disorder from major depressive disorder by assessing whether there has been a sustained two-week period of pervasive depressive mood.
doctor.question: During this past eight months, was there ever a period of two weeks in a row when you felt down or depressed most of the day nearly every day?

target_item.reason: The question is specifically about a two-week period of depressed mood nearly every day, which is not directly covered by the provided symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
I don’t know if I can say that clearly. Two weeks in a row, most of the day nearly every day… that’s pretty specific, and I’d have to think hard about it.

I’ve had low days, definitely, and times where I felt worn down or kind of flat, but whether it was truly depressed most of the day almost every day for a full two weeks… I’m not sure. I don’t want to overstate it. Sometimes the days blur together, especially when there’s stress at home, and then looking back I can’t always tell if I was actually down the whole time or just tired and fed up.

So I guess my honest answer is: I’m not sure. I can’t point to a definite two-week stretch like that, but I also wouldn’t say I’ve felt great the whole time.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there has been a distinct two-week major depressive episode, which best separates adjustment disorder/burnout from major depressive disorder or recurrent depression.
doctor.question: During the last eight months, was there ever a two-week period when you had almost no interest or pleasure in things nearly every day?

target_item.name: Negative_Symptoms
target_item.manifestation: What finally brought me in is that I feel like the part of me that used to reach for people and take pleasure in my work, yoga, galleries, even journaling, has gone very quiet, and I’m mostly just moving through obligations.
target_item.reason: The question is asking about loss of interest or pleasure, which is most directly covered by the negative symptoms profile, especially diminished motivation, social interest, and pleasure.

patient.answer:
Yes… I think that’s closer to what finally made me feel like I should come in, honestly. I don’t know if I can map it perfectly onto a clean two-week block, but there have definitely been stretches where the part of me that used to reach for things has just gone very quiet.

I used to be someone who would want to connect with people, or I’d get something out of my work, even when it was hard. I’d go to yoga, or wander through galleries, or write in my journal and feel like there was some pleasure or meaning in it. Lately it’s more like I know those things are supposed to matter to me, and I can remember that they used to, but I don’t really feel pulled toward them.

It’s not that I’m refusing everything or lying in bed all day. I still do what I have to do. I show up, I handle obligations, I go through the motions. But that’s kind of the problem — it feels like mostly obligations. The interest, the enjoyment, the part of me that used to naturally lean toward life a bit… it feels muted. So yes, I’d say there have been periods where I had very little interest or pleasure nearly every day, even if I’m hesitant about the exact timing.

doctor.intent: Clarify whether there has been a distinct major depressive episode by assessing a core vegetative symptom, which best separates adjustment disorder/burnout from major depressive disorder given confirmed anhedonia but unclear depressed mood.
doctor.question: During those stretches when your interest and pleasure were very low, did your sleep change noticeably?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking specifically about noticeable changes in sleep during periods of low interest or pleasure, but the provided symptom profile does not include a sleep-related symptom item.

patient.answer:
I’m not totally sure, honestly. I mean, my sleep is one of those things I don’t track very carefully unless it gets really extreme, and I don’t know that I could say there was a clear, noticeable change that lined up neatly with those stretches.

There were nights where I probably stayed up too late, but sometimes that’s just me avoiding the end of the day, if that makes sense, or getting caught in my own thoughts. And other times I’d sleep and still not feel especially refreshed. But I don’t know if that’s a sleep change exactly, or just being tired in a more general way.

So… I wouldn’t say I noticed a major change. Nothing where I thought, “Oh, I’m barely sleeping,” or “I’m sleeping all day.” It was more that the days felt kind of dull and heavy, but I can’t clearly tie that to my sleep being different.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there was a major depressive episode by checking for another core vegetative symptom beyond anhedonia, helping distinguish depressive disorder from adjustment disorder or burnout.
doctor.question: During those periods when your interest and pleasure were very low, did your appetite change noticeably?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about appetite changes during periods of low interest/pleasure, but the symptom profile does not include appetite or weight/appetite-related symptoms.

patient.answer:
I don’t think so… not in a way I noticed clearly. Appetite is a little tricky for me because it can vary day to day anyway — sometimes if I’m busy or tense I’ll forget to eat until later, and other times I’ll eat something just because it’s there, not because I’m especially hungry. So I’m hesitant to say there was a real change.

During those low-interest periods, I wasn’t really thinking, “Oh, I’ve lost my appetite,” or “I’m eating much more than usual.” It was more like food became part of the general routine — make something, eat enough, move on. I don’t remember my weight changing or people commenting or anything like that.

So… no, I wouldn’t say my appetite changed noticeably. If it did shift a little, it wasn’t enough that it stood out to me.

doctor.intent: Assess whether the patient has low energy/fatigue during the low-interest periods to clarify whether criteria for a major depressive episode are met versus adjustment-related distress or burnout.
doctor.question: During those periods when your interest and pleasure were very low, did you also feel unusually tired or low in energy?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking specifically about fatigue or low energy during low-interest periods, and the provided symptom profile does not include a distinct fatigue/energy symptom.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure I’d call it unusually tired, exactly. I mean… I did feel kind of drained sometimes, but it’s hard for me to separate that from just the emotional flatness of those periods, if that makes sense.

There were days where everything took more effort than it should have — answering messages, getting through work, doing normal chores — but I don’t remember it as a clear physical exhaustion, like I couldn’t get out of bed or needed to nap all the time. It was more like I had to manually push myself through things because there wasn’t much internal momentum.

So… maybe a little low energy, but I’m hesitant to say it was a big, noticeable change. It didn’t stand out to me the way the lack of interest did.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient had impaired concentration/indecisiveness during the low-interest periods, to clarify whether criteria for a major depressive episode are met versus adjustment disorder/burnout.
doctor.question: During those periods when your interest and pleasure were very low, did you have trouble concentrating?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking specifically about trouble concentrating during periods of low interest and pleasure, but the provided symptom profile does not include a concentration or cognitive-attention symptom item.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure I can say that I did, at least not in a clean way. Concentration is one of those things where I second-guess myself, because some days I’m focused and some days I’m not, and it depends so much on the task and how much structure there is around me.

During those low-interest stretches, I definitely had less drive to engage with things, so if something felt boring or optional, my mind would drift more easily. But I don’t know if that was concentration trouble exactly, or more that I just didn’t care enough to stay with it. Like, if I had to do something important, I could usually make myself sit down and get through it, even if it felt kind of mechanical.

I don’t remember it being a big obvious problem, like reading the same paragraph over and over or not being able to follow conversations. Nothing that stood out that strongly. So I’d say… maybe a little harder to stay engaged, but I wouldn’t say I noticed major concentration problems.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient has had feelings of worthlessness or excessive guilt during the low-interest periods, which would help distinguish a major depressive episode from adjustment disorder or burnout.
doctor.question: During those stretches when your interest and pleasure were very low, did you feel worthless or excessively guilty?

target_item.reason: The question asks about feelings of worthlessness or excessive guilt, which are depressive-cognition symptoms and are not covered by the provided schizophrenia symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
I don’t think so… not in the way I would understand “worthless” or “excessively guilty.” I mean, I can be hard on myself in general, and during those stretches I might think, “Why am I not doing more?” or “Why does everything feel so flat when nothing is technically wrong?” But I don’t remember it turning into this strong belief that I was a bad person or that I didn’t deserve anything.

And guilt… maybe ordinary guilt, like if I wasn’t as responsive to people or I let something sit too long, I’d feel a little bad about that. But it wasn’t this heavy, consuming guilt, like I’d done something terrible or was responsible for things beyond me. It was more frustration with myself than guilt, I think.

So no, I wouldn’t say I felt worthless. Maybe self-critical at times, but not in a severe or constant way.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there was a definite two-week period of depressed mood, which would help distinguish a depressive episode from adjustment-related or burnout presentations.
doctor.question: At any point in the last eight months, was there a period of at least two weeks when you felt sad, down, or depressed nearly every day?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about a sustained period of depressed mood nearly every day, which is not covered by the provided schizophrenia symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
I don’t think there was a full two-week stretch like that, no. I’ve had days where I felt kind of down or emotionally heavy, and there were those periods where things felt flat and I wasn’t getting much pleasure out of things, but “sad or depressed nearly every day” feels a little different to me.

I’m trying to be careful because I know it can blur together when you look back over eight months. But when I think of actually feeling sad — like waking up most days feeling depressed, or carrying that low mood through the day — I don’t remember that happening for two weeks straight. It was more intermittent, or more like lack of interest than sadness, if that distinction makes sense.

So my best answer would be no, not that I noticed.

doctor.intent: Clarify whether the symptoms are persisting because of an identifiable ongoing stressor, which would favor adjustment disorder over depressive, anxiety, dysthymic, or burnout diagnoses.
doctor.question: If your older relative were no longer living with you, do you think these symptoms would mostly go away?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This whole change in how I’m thinking, working, and connecting with people has been going on for about eight months, since we took my older relative into our apartment.
target_item.reason: The question asks whether the symptoms are tied to the living situation with the older relative, which is the context given for when the overall eight-month change began.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure they would mostly go away, exactly. I do think the timing is hard to ignore, because this whole change in how I’ve been thinking, working, and connecting with people has really been going on for about eight months, and that’s basically since we took my older relative into our apartment.

So part of me thinks, yes, if that living situation changed, maybe some of the pressure around it would ease up. But I don’t know that I can say everything would just return to normal automatically. It’s been long enough now that it feels like it’s affected my routines and how I move through the day, not just a temporary reaction to one bad week.

I guess my answer is: I think it’s connected to having them there, because that’s when it started, but I can’t confidently say it would all mostly disappear if they weren’t living with us anymore.

final_diagnosis.reason: Symptoms began in clear temporal relation to an identifiable ongoing psychosocial stressor (older relative moving into the home) and have caused functional decline. The presentation is dominated by reduced interest/pleasure, emotional flatness, and strain, but criteria for a major depressive episode are not clearly met because persistent depressed mood was denied and additional neurovegetative/cognitive symptoms were not established. Generalized anxiety disorder is also not supported because excessive anxiety/worry more days than not for at least 6 months was not confirmed. Burnout is less fitting because the stressor is primarily home/family-based rather than occupational.
